heading: What a native service reaches
body:
Native services use their platform SDK (software development kit). They inject an ApplicationEventPublisher for local events that they own. They use OnEvent, and OnStart and OnStop for the lifecycle. Each example initializes the service and publishes a CatalogCount model. A listener updates the count, and cleanup resets it. Old callbacks from an earlier activation cannot change the owners that replaced it. A native service has no page, so it cannot use Tachyon's browser APIs (such as `Clock`, `Clipboard` or `Geolocation`) or listen for their built-in event models (such as `ConnectivityChanged`). The build refuses them in a service that is linked into the app (`TY1317`). Use them in a JavaScript, TypeScript or WebAssembly service, and send the result to the native service with an event. `WindowControls` is the one exception: a linked service gets it from the host through an uninitialized `WindowControls` field with `Needs` or `NeedsAll` (ADR 0089; see the feature "What a page may do to its window"). A linked service may also listen for `ApplicationStateChanged`, because the app sends it, not the page (see "Background and foreground"). Only Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust services are linked into a native app. JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, Go, Ruby, Java, F#, Lua, Python and C++ services always run in the page, also inside a native app, so this section has no tab for them.

On macOS, Linux and Windows, a page call sends a JSON request and waits for a reply. The Rust method runs synchronously on the host's user interface thread: the macOS main actor, the Linux GTK main loop, or the Windows window thread. Windows sends one call at a time with a 10 second timeout. Keep these methods short and put long work in an application-owned background task. Arguments are positional; a model argument uses its Rust field names as JSON keys. Same-named methods in mutually exclusive `#[cfg]` implementation blocks pass the class-layout checks, and the target compiler selects the matching implementation.

A desktop bridge request is at most 64 KiB. Linux and Windows also cap the encoded reply at 64 KiB and answer an oversized reply with a paging hint. macOS currently has no reply-size cap. Application code owns paging and its total-transfer limit, for example 2 MiB; these are not fields of the Tachyon bridge. Keep each text page at most 24 KiB and check that the complete escaped JSON reply fits the host limit: quotes and backslashes double in JSON, and control characters can expand further. The Linux bridge fixture verifies quote/backslash, multibyte and plain-text pages, plus oversized request and reply refusal.

Tachyon imposes no sandbox root on Linux or Windows. Apps choose their own per-user paths, such as `%LOCALAPPDATA%\<app>` on Windows and `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` or `$XDG_STATE_HOME` on Linux. MSIX and Flatpak packaging are not planned.
